https://doi.org/10.1038/s41590-026-02637-w Article Innate immune imprints shape HIV-1 reservoir cell persistence during long-term antiretroviral therapy

Host immune responses that can target and eliminate HIV-1 reservoir cells during suppressive antiretroviral therapy are poorly understood. Here, analyzing over 6,000 proviral DNA amplicons from 104 individuals on long-term antiretroviral therapy, we found that carriers of HLA-C2 allotypes, which promote NK cell education via interactions with KIR2DL1, exhibited lower frequencies of intact proviruses. No protective effects of HLA-C2 alleles were observed during untreated infection, suggesting a selective vulnerability of reservoir cells to NK-cell-mediated immune activity under antiretroviral therapy. Supporting this, frequencies of KIR2DL1+ NK cells, particularly those coexpressing the activating HLA-E receptor NKG2C, were inversely correlated with frequencies of intact proviruses. Moreover, viral protein U variants that strongly downregulate HLA-C, increasing a missing-self response by KIR2DL1+ NK cells, were associated with smaller reservoirs in carriers of HLA-C2. Infected cells surviving long-term displayed elevated HLA-C expression, consistent with in vivo selection for resistance to KIR2DL1+ NK-cell-mediated immune clearance. Immune activity of KIR2DL1+ NK cells against viral reservoir cells was enhanced by NKG2C–HLA-E interactions, as sequence variants in HLA-E-restricted HIV-1 epitopes reduced NKG2C-dependent NK cell activation and were associated with higher frequencies of intact proviruses. These findings underscore the critical influence of host and viral genetic variation on reservoir persistence and highlight opportunities for leveraging innate immunity in HIV cure strategies.

For this purpose, we used single-genome, near-full-length proviral next-generation sequencing28 to characterize the frequencies of genome-intact and genome-defective proviruses in a cohort of n = 104 study participants who live with HIV-1 (PLWH) and had received ART for a median of 21 (range: 10–27) years at the time of peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) collection (Supplementary Table 1). In total, these experiments identified n = 6,077 HIV-1 DNA amplification products, of which n = 366 were defined as genome-intact, using a previously described computational code7 (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Approximately 38.25% (n = 140) of these genome-intact proviruses were identified only once in a given study participant, while 61.75% (n = 226) of proviruses were detected at least two times in individual study participants and represented members of proviral clones that result from the proliferative turnover of HIV-1-infected cells29–32. Annotating this dataset with corresponding high-resolution HLA class I typing data demonstrated that HLA-B*57 and HLA-B*27, which restrict immunodominant HIV-1-specific cytotoxic T cell responses and are associated with protection against HIV-1 disease progression during untreated infection33, were not associated with lower frequencies of intact HIV-1 proviruses during suppressive ART (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Moreover, HLA-B*35Px alleles, which are associated with accelerated HIV-1 disease progression during untreated infection34, showed no influence on HIV-1 reservoir size (Extended Data Fig. 2b). However, subsequent analysis demonstrated marked reductions of intact proviruses in carriers of HLA class I alleles influencing NK cell education. In particular, individuals with at least one HLA-C2 allotype, which promotes strong NK cell education through high-avidity interactions with KIR2DL1 (refs. 35,36), had significantly lower frequencies of intact proviruses compared to study participants carrying only HLA-C1 alleles (Fig. 1b); this was true when all intact proviruses were counted, when clonal intact proviral sequences were only counted once and when results were adjusted for race or for the presence of the protective (HLA-B*57 and HLA-B*27) or disease-accelerating (HLA-B*35Px) alleles (Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2c). A similar observation was made for carriers of at least one HLA-B Bw4 (BBw4) allotype (Fig. 1c), which can support NK cell education through interactions with KIR3DL137–39; these individuals displayed significantly reduced frequencies of intact proviruses relative to study persons without BBw4 alleles, independently of HLA-B*57, HLA-B*27 and HLA-B*35Px expression or race (Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2c). Rebound-competent HIV-1-infected cells can persist life-long despite currently available antiretroviral therapy (ART), and represent the major barrier to the development of curative treatment interventions for HIV-1 infection1–3. The majority of these persisting viral reservoir cells include memory CD4+ T cells that harbor a chromosomally integrated form of viral DNA as a ‘provirus’, but express limited viral RNA and effectively resist immune elimination, for reasons that are currently poorly understood4. Nevertheless, several recent experimental observations suggest that the human immune system can recognize and target some of these reservoir cells, likely due to ongoing low-level viral transcription5–9 during ART. Indeed, imprints of host immune selection pressure can be detected through deep interrogations of the viral reservoir cell pool, specifically when focusing on genome-intact proviruses, which decay faster after ART initiation10,11 and appear more susceptible to host immune activity. In particular, the profiling of chromosomal integration sites has indicated the selective persistence of genome-intact proviruses in heterochromatin locations, likely as a result of immune-mediated selection pressure that preferentially targets more transcriptionally active proviruses integrated into accessible chromatin7,12–14. Moreover, single-cell proteogenomic profiling studies suggested that, relative to the total memory CD4+ T cell pool, persisting viral reservoir cells express higher levels of inhibitory immunoregulatory markers15, a finding that is best explained by effective immune targeting of reservoir cells with a phenotypic profile more conducive to antiviral immune activity. The types of host immune responses that can effectively drive immune selection of HIV-1 reservoir cells, however, are unclear at present. Cytotoxic T cells can eliminate infected cells when presenting viral peptides on human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules and have a recognized role in antiviral immunity during untreated HIV-1 infection16, especially in persons with natural, drug-free control of HIV-1 replication17–19; however, their ability to target HIV-1 reservoir cells during ART is less well understood20. Natural killer (NK) cells preferentially recognize and kill HLA-deficient target cells, providing a complementary mode of immune surveillance. NK cells undergo education through interactions between inhibitory killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIR) and corresponding HLA class I ligands21 and can contribute to antiviral immune defense in untreated HIV-1 infection22,23; however, recent studies also suggest their involvement in immune activity against viral reservoirs during ART24–26, and during drug-free HIV-1 control following ART interruption in rare ‘posttreatment controllers’27. Here we conducted a detailed characterization of proviral sequences and host immune responses in a large cohort of people living with HIV-1 on long-term ART to define immune mechanisms that can impose selection pressure against the HIV-1 reservoir cell pool.

No differences in HIV-1 reservoir sizes were detected between carriers of KIR-A and KIR-B haplotypes (Extended Data Fig. 2d); moreover, the presence of HLA-A Bw4 allotypes (ABw4) was not associated with altered viral reservoir size, consistent with prior studies suggesting that HLA-A Bw4 alleles do not effectively contribute to NK cell education41 and represent functionally weaker ligands for KIR3DL142 (Extended Data Fig. 2e). Together, these investigations strongly support the hypothesis that viral reservoir sizes during long-term ART are influenced and modulated by immunogenetic characteristics impacting NK cell education.

No protective effects of HLA-C2 during untreated HIV-1 infection Because associations between HLA class I alleles and frequencies of intact proviruses during long-term ART could reflect immune effects occurring before the initiation of therapy33,43, we examined relationships between the HLA-C2 and BBw4 alleles and plasma viral loads in PLWH not treated with ART. Among n = 4,007 ART-naive study participants recruited in a previous cohort study44, HLA-C2 was not associated with reduced plasma viremia, regardless of coexpression of the protective HLA class I alleles (B*57, B*27 and B*35Px) or race (Fig. 1e and Table 2). HLA-B Bw4 alleles correlated with lower viral loads; however, this effect was no longer detectable after adjusting for race and HLA-B*57, HLA-B*27 or HLA-B*35Px carrier status (Fig. 1e and Table 2). Combined presence or absence of HLA-C2 and HLA-B Bw4 was also unrelated to viral loads in untreated individuals after excluding carriers of HLA-B*27 and HLA-B*57 (Fig. 1e). By contrast, in our independent cohort of n = 104 individuals on long-term ART, the effects of HLA-C2 and HLA-B Bw4 on viral reservoir size remained detectable after adjusting for the presence of HLA-B*57, HLA-B*27 and HLA-B*35Px or race (Table 1

and Extended Data Fig. 2c). Together, these findings indicate that the associations between HLA-C2 and/or HLA-BBw4 and the frequencies of intact proviruses during long-term ART likely reflect immune pressure specifically acting on reservoir cells under suppressive therapy rather than effects established before ART initiation.

KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1−NKG2C+ NK cells inversely correlate with HIV-1 reservoir size To explore mechanisms underlying the immunogenetic associations between HLA-C2 and/or BBw4 alleles and lower frequencies of intact proviruses, we initially evaluated the magnitude of HIV-1 Gag-specific T cell responses in a subgroup of PLWH on ART who jointly carried at least one C2 allele and one BBw4 allele, or none of these two types of alleles (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). However, using established assays to quantify the frequencies of HIV-1-specific CD8+ T cells expressing the cytokines IFN-γ, TNF or IL-2, or the degranulation marker CD107a/b, we observed that the proportions and polyfunctionality of Gag-specific CD8+ T cells were statistically unrelated to HLA-C2 or BBw4 carrier status, and not correlated with the frequencies of intact HIV-1 proviruses (Extended Data Fig. 3a–c). Moreover, HIV-1-specific CD8+ T cells that expressed perforin or granzyme A and B in response to Gag stimulation were not different between HLA-C2 and BBw4 co-carriers and individuals lacking such alleles (Extended Data Fig. 3d). CD8+ T cell responses recognizing CMV pp65 and IE-1, analyzed for control purposes, also did not vary significantly between individuals with or without C2 and BBw4 alleles (Extended Data Fig. 3a–d). As a subsequent step, we conducted a deep phenotypic characterization of NK cells in these study persons using a multiparametric spectral flow cytometry analysis involving 22 NK cell surface markers (Supplementary Table 4). These studies demonstrated that, relative to C2 and BBw4 double-negative study persons, C2 and BBw4 double-positive individuals on ART had significantly higher levels of NK cells expressing the HLA-C2 receptor KIR2DL1; moreover, proportions of these KIR2DL1+ NK cells, when assessed either within the total NK pool or within the highly cytotoxic CD56dimCD16+ NK population, were inversely correlated with the frequencies of intact proviruses (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). A closer examination revealed that the link between KIR2DL1+ NK cells and reservoir sizes was confined to the KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1− subset, which exhibited an inverse correlation with frequencies of intact proviruses (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 4b). In contrast, the proportions of total KIR3DL1+, KIR2DL1−KIR3DL1+ or KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1+ NK cells were not different between C2 and BBw4 co-carriers and noncarriers, and did not correlate with frequencies of intact proviruses; this was true when assessed within total NK cells or within the cytotoxic CD56dimCD16+ NK cell subset (Fig. 2c–e and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). In a subsequent phenotypic characterization of KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1− NK cells, we observed that these cells frequently coexpress the activating HLA-E receptor CD94/NKG2C (termed ‘NKG2C’ in this paper)45 (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f), a marker that denotes a subset of ‘adaptive’ NK cells46,47. In particular, we noted that KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1−NKG2C+ NK cells, a cell population reminiscent of single KIR+ adaptive NK cells previously described in oncologic contexts48,49, were selectively expanded in HLA-C2 carriers and inversely associated with the frequencies of intact proviruses (Fig. 2f). By contrast, proportions of NK cells expressing KIR2DL1 in the absence of NKG2C, or NKG2C in the absence of KIR2DL1, were not correlated with frequencies of intact proviruses and not quantitatively different between individuals with or without HLA-C2 (Fig. 2g,h). Interestingly, KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1− NK cells also frequently coexpressed DNAM-1, CD57 and KLRG1, while exhibiting limited surface expression of the inhibitory HLA-E receptor NKG2A (Extended Data Fig. 4i), consistent with some of the previously recognized phenotypic features of adaptive NK cells50. Moreover, KIR2DL1+ NK cells coexpressing NKG2A did not differ between HLA-C2 carriers and noncarriers, while KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1−NKG2A− NK cells, a cell population enriched for KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1−NKG2C+ cells, were expanded in HLA-C2 carriers and correlated inversely with the frequency of intact proviruses (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). Notably, inverse correlations involving KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1−NKG2C+ NK cells were observed when clonal intact proviruses were counted only once (Fig. 2a–h) or when scored individually (Extended Data Fig. 5). In sum, these observations identify KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1−NKG2C+ NK cells as the subset with the most definitive inverse association with intact proviral reservoir size, suggesting that both KIR2DL1–HLA-C2-mediated NK cell education and NKG2C– HLA-E-driven NK cell activation contribute to shaping the innate cellular immune responses against persisting HIV-1 reservoir cells.

The HLA-B21 M/T signal peptide polymorphism, previously shown to influence HLA-E surface stabilization60, was not associated with the proportion of KIR2DL1+KIR3DL1−NKG2C+ NK cells nor with the frequency of intact HIV-1 proviruses in our cohort of PLWH on long-term ART (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g). Since NKG2C–HLA-E interactions can influence NK cell responses against CMV through variant-specific recognition of the canonical CMV UL40-encoded VL9 peptide56,61–64, we next investigated whether sequence variations in HIV-1-derived, noncanonical HLA-E-restricted epitopes can impact HIV-1 reservoir size through peptide- or peptide-variant-specific NKG2C engagement during prolonged ART. To address this, we analyzed the amino acid diversity in previously characterized HLA-E-restricted HIV-1 epitopes47,65,66 within autologous near-full-length proviral sequences from our original cohort of study participants on ART (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6a,b,d). We observed that the E460A Gag variant, located at the HLA-E anchor position 9 of the peptide RPEPTAPPE, was strongly associated with higher frequencies of intact proviruses in HLA-C2 carriers, but not in HLA-C2-negative individuals; moreover,

a similar observation was made for the R747P variant, located at position 1 in the HLA-E restricted Env epitope RLVDGFLAL. In addition, for two other previously characterized HLA-E epitopes in Gag, we noted higher reservoirs associated with amino acid variations at the NKG2C contact residues67 at position 6 (A340G in KALGPAATL) and position 8 (Y79F in SEELRSLYN), although these differences did not reach statistical significance for the KALGPAATL epitope. Nonetheless, our findings suggest that effective NKG2C-mediated activation appears to require concurrent missing-self-recognition signals mediated through KIR2DL1, providing a mechanistic explanation for why sequence variations in HLA-E epitopes preferentially influence HIV-1 reservoir size in individuals with KIR2DL1–HLA-C2-dependent NK cell education.

Vpu sequence variations influence HIV-1 reservoirs To assess the in vivo impact of KIR2DL1+NKG2C+ NK cells on the HIV-1 reservoir, we investigated whether genetic variations in Vpu correlate with proviral reservoir size. Prior studies71,73 have shown that the capacity of Vpu to downregulate HLA-C depends on amino acid residues 2, 3, 5, 15, 16 and 24 within the Vpu sequence, which interact with the HLA-C transmembrane domain to reduce surface expression (Fig. 5a). A higher number of Vpu residues known to downregulate HLA-C in autologous near-full-length proviruses correlated with lower frequencies of intact proviruses (Fig. 5b), consistent with NK-cell-mediated immune pressure on reservoir cells. This relationship was restricted to HLA-C2 carriers and was not observed in individuals lacking HLA-C2, suggesting that Vpu-mediated HLA-C downregulation preferentially sensitizes

reservoir cells to clearance by KIR2DL1-educated NK cells. Combined analyses further supported a cooperative effect between Vpu-driven HLA-C downregulation and NKG2C–HLA-E-dependent NK cell activation in HLA-C2 carriers, as the largest reservoirs were observed in individuals harboring Vpu variants with limited HLA-C downregulation capacity together with variants in HLA-E-restricted epitopes exhibiting reduced NKG2C engagement (Fig. 5c). Conversely, higher reservoir sizes associated with unfavorable HLA-E epitope variants were partially mitigated by Vpu sequences retaining strong HLA-C downregulation activity. Consistent with these findings, a combined host–proviral genetic polymorphism analysis demonstrated that frequencies of intact proviruses between carriers of the most and the least favorable viral and host sequence polymorphisms in HLA-C, Vpu and HLA-E-restricted HIV-1 epitopes differed by more than sevenfold, equivalent to the decay of intact proviruses observed over 10 years of continuous ART, assuming a half-life of intact proviruses of 44 months74,75 (Fig. 5d). These results suggest that coordinated HLA-C-dependent education and NKG2C–HLA-E-dependent activation act synergistically to mediate NK-cell-driven reduction of HIV-1 reservoir cells in vivo.

HLA-C expression on HIV-1 reservoir cells For additional validation of in vivo NK-cell-driven immune effects against HIV-1 reservoir cells, we used a single-cell proteogenomic profiling assay, termed PheP-Seq in our prior work15,76, to track the longitudinal evolution of HLA-C surface expression on CD4+ T cells harboring intact HIV-1 proviruses. Specifically, we analyzed samples from two individuals homozygous for HLA-C1 and two individuals homozygous for HLA-C2, using PBMCs collected approximately one year and 17–20 years after the initiation of suppressive ART. In brief, memory CD4+ T cells were isolated and stained with oligonucleotide-tagged antibodies targeting surface proteins, followed by single-cell encapsulation and barcoding using a microfluidics platform. Each cell then underwent multiplex PCR to amplify 18 discrete HIV-1 genomic regions (200–300 bp each; totaling ~4,000 bp), including two sites previously shown to be predictive of viral genome intactness77. Amplification products were then pooled, sequenced and computationally deconvoluted to assign sequencing reads to their individual input cells. In total, we analyzed 310,438 and 345,635 memory CD4+ T cells from study participants carrying the HLA-C1 or HLA-C2 alleles, respectively. Based on established criteria, 958 and 577 of these cells were classified as HIV-1-infected cells harboring any form of provirus, while 83 and 63 cells were identified as containing intact proviruses in carriers of C1 or C2 alleles, respectively (Fig. 5e). This high-resolution analytical approach revealed no significant differences in HLA-C surface expression between CD4+ T cells harboring intact proviruses and uninfected total memory CD4+ T cells within one year of ART initiation, regardless of the HLA-C subgroup (Fig. 5f). However, after long-term ART, we observed that in carriers of HLA-C2, but not of HLA-C1, HLA-C surface expression was higher in CD4+ T cells harboring intact HIV-1 compared with the overall memory CD4+ T cell population. In contrast, surface expression of alternative classical and nonclassical HLA class I alleles did not differ between cells containing intact proviruses and the total memory CD4+ T cell pool at any time point (Fig. 5f). Interestingly, in HLA-C1 carriers, HIV-1-infected cells displayed reduced surface expression of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C at one year after ART initiation, possibly suggesting adaptation to CTL-mediated immune selection pressure during early stages of ART; however, this was not detectable at later time points, consistent with limited effects of CTL on viral reservoir cells during long-term ART. Together, these findings support the hypothesis that heightened in vivo immune selection pressure in HLA-C2 carriers preferentially eliminates infected cells with low HLA-C expression, leading to the enrichment of reservoir cells with high HLA-C expression levels and an increased likelihood of evading immune-mediated clearance by KIR2DL1-educated NK cells.

Our analysis, to our knowledge one of the most comprehensive integrative analyses of proviral reservoir cell sequences, host immunogenetic factors and antiviral immune responses conducted so far, challenges this paradigm. Our findings suggest that instead, the size of the viral reservoir during long-term ART is regulated by a finely balanced interplay between infected cells and innate cellular immunity. In particular, our data suggest that NK cells educated via KIR2DL1, considered as the strongest driver of NK cell education due to the high avidity and low peptide selectivity of KIR2DL1–HLA-C2 interactions79, can exert effective immune selection pressure on the reservoir cell pool, specifically when concurrently activated through peptide-variant-specific NKG2C–HLA-E interactions. This model points to a distinct vulnerability of reservoir cells to NK-cell-mediated recognition, presumably at least in part driven by residual Vpu expression. Even at low levels, Vpu may downregulate HLA-C in reservoir cells when favorable viral residues are present, thereby generating a missing-self NK cell recognition signal on KIR2DL1+ NK cells that can then be further amplified through NKG2C-dependent recognition of HLA-E-restricted HIV-1 epitopes. Of note, it is also plausible, if not likely, that differential recognition of HLA-E-restricted CMV epitopes61 further influenced activation of KIR2DL1+NKG2C+ NK cell populations in our study participants; however, our study design did not allow for an assessment of CMV sequence variations to more definitively investigate this. Our proposed model does not diminish the importance of HIV-1-specific T cells in recognizing and eliminating HIV-1-infected cells, particularly during untreated infection or treatment interruptions, when full viral replication cycles occur and T cell-driven immune pressure shapes viral sequence evolution within targeted epitopes80. Rather, our findings suggest a functional dichotomy in which HIV-1-specific T cell responses dominate immune selection during active viral replication off ART, whereas NK-cell-mediated mechanisms become the prevailing form of immune pressure on the viral reservoir under long-term suppressive ART. Notably, our study focused on individuals with very long durations of antiretroviral treatment (median duration of 21 years), and we excluded participants with shorter treatment durations (<10 years). Whether NK cells exert measurable selection pressure on reservoir cells during earlier phases of ART remains unclear and will require investigation in future longitudinal studies. It is also conceivable that mechanisms of immune selection shift progressively over the course of ART, with HIV-1-specific T cells possibly representing a driving force of immune selection during earlier stages of ART, when many proviruses are integrated in genic regions and display higher levels of transcriptional activity7,12, potentially enabling immune recognition by T cell receptor-dependent mechanisms at this time. Cells that survive and persist beyond this phase may do so by acquiring immune-evasive features such as HLA class I downregulation; these adaptations, while protective against cytotoxic T lymphocytes, might reciprocally confer increased vulnerability to NK-cell-mediated elimination, effectively shifting the dominant form of immune pressure to NK cells as treatment continues. Such a cooperative dynamic between T cells and NK cells, each exerting complementary but temporally distinct selection pressures on the viral reservoir, warrants further exploration in future longitudinal studies. The precise role of NK cells educated by mechanisms other than HLA-C2–KIR2DL1, such as NK cell education via HLA-Bw4–KIR3DL1 and HLA-E–NKG2A, at earlier stages of ART also merits additional investigation. Of note, the findings presented are concordant with prior studies suggesting a role for KIR-educated NK cells in posttreatment controllers27, and additional future studies exploring the role of NK cells in immune-mediated posttreatment control of HIV-1 replication would likely be highly informative. While our data suggest heightened immune activity of KIR2DL1+NKG2C+ NK cells against persisting HIV-1-infected cells, consistent with the promising therapeutic activity of single-KIR+

adaptive NK cells against KIR–HLA-mismatched leukemia cells48,49,81,82, we emphasize that they cannot eradicate viral reservoir cells; rather, surviving reservoir cells appear to adapt by sustaining high-level HLA-C expression, enabling resistance to KIR2DL1+ NK cell clearance. Elimination of such a highly selected reservoir cell pool will likely require more targeted interventions that specifically disassemble this protective layer of the reservoir, possibly through pharmacological manipulation of KIR2DL1–HLA-C2-dependent immune checkpoints83,84; however, we hypothesize that the profound resilience of HIV-1 reservoir cells may require simultaneous targeting of additional viral vulnerabilities. Importantly, our data strongly supports the hypothesis that viral reservoir cell persistence is heavily influenced by genetic variability within both the host genome and proviral sequences, suggesting that larger cohort studies focusing on integrated assessments of viral and host genetic diversity will yield deeper insight into vulnerabilities and susceptibilities of the reservoir cell pool. When sufficiently powered, such studies may help to disentangle more complex immunogenetic interactions between viral and host sequence variations, including combinatorial effects that were beyond the scope of our study, and may also reveal specific reservoir cell dynamics more definitively associated with age and sex85. Ultimately, broader characterizations of viral reservoirs, integrated with evaluations of host and viral genetic variation, will enable more personalized assessments of reservoir biology and may help identify individuals most likely to benefit from precision interventions tailored to specific viral and host factors.

Methods Study participants Study participants living with HIV-1 on ART were recruited at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, the University of California at San Francisco, Case Western Reserve University, the Women’s Interagency HIV Study (WHIS) and the AIDS Clinical Trials Group (ACTG protocol A5321). No formal sample size calculations, randomizations or investigator blinding operations were performed. Clinical and demographic characteristics of the study participants are summarized in Supplementary Table 1. All study participants provided written consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki before enrolment. Depending on the individual source protocols, study participants were eligible to receive a small stipend for transportation and meal expenses. PBMC samples were collected according to protocols approved by the respective Institutional Review Boards. Data from treatment-naive PLWH were available from a total of n = 4,007 study persons from the following US cohorts44: AIDS Clinical Trials Group (ACTG, https://actgnetwork.org), ALIVE, HIV Natural History Study (DoD HIV NHS, http://idcrp.usuhs.edu), Ragon Institute Controller Cohort (https://www.broadinstitute.org/hiv-controllers/internationalhiv-controllers-study), Study on the Consequences of Protease Inhibitor Era (SCOPE, https://clinicaltrials.ucsf.edu/trial/NCT00187512). Each participant approved the use of their DNA samples for genetic analysis.

Near full-length proviral sequencing Genomic DNA from study participants was subjected to HIV-1 near-full-genome amplification using a non-multiplexed single-amplicon as described previously28,86. All near-full-length PCR products were subjected to Illumina MiSeq sequencing at the MGH DNA Core facility. Resulting Illumina short reads were de novo assembled using Ultracycler v1.0 and aligned to HXB2 to identify large deleterious deletions (<8,000 bp of the amplicon aligned to HXB2), out-of-frame indels, premature or lethal stop codons, internal inversions, or packaging signal deletions (≥15 bp insertions and/or deletions relative to HXB2), using an automated in-house pipeline written in Python programming language (https://github.com/BWH-Lichterfeld-Lab/ Intactness-Pipeline). The presence or absence of APOBEC-3G- and 3F-associated hypermutations was determined using the Los Alamos HIV Sequence Database Hypermut 2.0 program. Viral sequences that lacked all mutations listed above were classified as ‘genome-intact’. Sequence alignments were performed using MAFFT in Geneious Prime software v2023.1 (https://www.geneious.com). Phylogenetic distances between sequences were examined using a PhyML tree87 in Geneious Prime software. Viral sequences were considered clonal if they had completely identical consensus sequences; single-nucleotide variations in primer binding sites were not considered for clonality analysis. For HIV-1 reservoir quantification, only sequences generated by a single-amplicon PCR approach were included in the analysis. In addition, proviral sequencing data generated by the five-amplicon approach, preceded by whole-genome amplification reactions86, were used when available in selected patients for analyzing proviral sequence diversity. For HIV-1 sequence polymorphism analysis, both HLA-E epitope and Vpu variant calling was performed using genome-intact proviruses; however, for individuals with fewer than three intact proviral sequences, both intact and available near-full-length defective sequences were analyzed to ensure that variant assessment accurately reflected the proviral sequence diversity of each study participant.

HLA class I and KIR typing High-resolution HLA class I and KIR typing were performed using a targeted next-generation sequencing method, as previously described88.

Serologic testing for CMV Testing for CMV IgG antibodies was performed using Arlington Scientific Cytomegalovirus IgG ELISA Test Kit (Cat#22-415-207) or the

Abbexa Cytomegalovirus IgG Rapid Test Kit (Cat#ABIN5708603), per the manufacturer’s instructions.

Phenotypic analysis of NK cells by flow cytometry PBMCs were thawed, stained with LIVE/DEAD Blue Viability Dye (Invitrogen) for 10 min and subsequently preincubated for 10 min with an Fc receptor (FcR) blocking reagent (Miltenyi Biotec). Afterward, cells were incubated for 25 min with different combinations of appropriately titrated antibodies directed against NK cell markers as listed in Supplementary Table 4. Subsequently, the cells were fixed in 2% paraformaldehyde in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and acquired on an Aurora spectral cytometer (Cytek Biosciences) at the Ragon Institute Flow Cytometry Core Facility. Data were analyzed using FlowJo v10.9.0 software (Tree Star LLC). Gating strategies are summarized in Extended Data Fig. 10a. Fluorescence minus one samples were prepared and used as part of the gating strategy (Extended Data Fig. 10b).

After stimulation, cells were washed and stained with LIVE/DEAD Blue Viability Dye (Invitrogen), followed by preincubation with 2 µl of FcR blocking reagent and surface staining for 25 min with appropriately titrated antibodies directed against T cell surface markers, as listed in Supplementary Table 5. Intracellular cytokine staining was performed with appropriately titrated antibodies directed against intracellular cytokines, as listed in Supplementary Table 5. The cells were fixed in 2% paraformaldehyde in PBS and acquired on a Cytek Aurora spectral cytometer (Cytek Biosciences). Fluorescence minus one samples were prepared and used as part of the gating strategy. Unstimulated controls were run for each sample and subtracted as background. ELISA-based HLA-E binding assays Peptide loading of peptide-free HLA-E complexes was performed as previously described, with minor modifications68. Briefly, peptide-free HLA-E–β2-microglobulin (β2M) complexes were generated by macro-refolding in the absence of peptide ligand. Refolding buffer consisted of 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 2 mM EDTA, 5 mM reduced glutathione and 0.5 mM oxidized glutathione. Peptide-loading was performed in polypropylene V-bottom 96-well plates (Greiner Bio-One) and incubated for 3 h on ice. Peptide-loaded HLA-E complexes were quantified using a sandwich ELISA as previously described64,68,92. High-binding 96-well plates (Life Technologies) were coated overnight at 4°C with anti-HLA-E monoclonal antibody (clone 3D12; BioLegend) at 10 μg ml−1 in coating buffer (BioLegend), washed in PBS and blocked with 2% IgG-free BSA (Sigma-Aldrich) for 2 h at room temperature. Peptide loading reactions were diluted 1:100 in 2% BSA, and 50 μl was added per well before incubation for 1 h at room temperature. Wells containing VL9 peptides were spatially separated to prevent cross-contamination. Following washing (0.05% Tween-20 wash buffer; BioLegend), bound complexes were detected using HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-human β2M antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 0.2 μg ml−1) for 30 min at 4°C. Signal was amplified using goat anti-rabbit HRP-conjugated IgG (EnVision+ System-HRP; Agilent; 1:15 dilution in 2% BSA containing 1% mouse serum) for 15 min at room temperature. Plates were developed using TMB substrate (BioLegend) for 10 min, stopped with H2SO4 stop solution (BioLegend); absorbance was measured at 450 nm.

Base pair variants in HLA-E-restricted Gag epitopes were inserted in the pNL4-3-dEnv plasmid, a kind gift from N. Manel and D. Littman (New York University, New York City, USA)93, to create Gag variant Y79F in the SN9 epitope, Gag variant A340G in the KL9 epitope and Gag variant E460A in the RE9 epitope by a commercial laboratory (Azenta). Plasmids containing all three of these HLA-E epitope variants associated with higher HIV-1 reservoir size or all three of the corresponding epitope sequences associated with lower HIV-1 reservoir size were then digested with the restriction enzymes BssHII and SbfI, and the resulting gag fragments were ligated into the pNL4-3 and pM4-5 backbones to generate four plasmids. Viral particles were produced by transfecting 293 T cells with the respective HIV-1 plasmids using Lipofectamine™ 3000 Transfection Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in Opti-MEM™ I reduced-serum medium per the manufacturer’s instructions. Supernatants containing infectious retroviruses were harvested 48 hours after transfection, quantified with the Lenti-X™ p24 Rapid Titer Kit (#631476, Takara) and stored at −80°C.

Functional NK cell assays Primary CD4+ T cells isolated by negative immunomagnetic enrichment kit (Miltenyi Biotec) were stimulated in RPMI medium supplemented with 10% fetal calf serum and recombinant IL-2 (100 IU ml−1) for three days with ImmunoCult™ Human CD3/CD28 T Cell Activator (#10971, Stemcell) at 25 μl ml−1, and then infected with the designated viral constructs at a multiplicity of infection of 0.1 for six hours. After 2 washes, cells were resuspended in medium and plated at 3–5 × 105 cells per well in a 24-well plate. Five days later, infected cells were enriched by depletion of CD4+ T cells using a positive immunomagnetic selection kit (#17852, Stemcell) and tested for HLA-C surface expression as described in the ‘Flow cytometric assessment of HLA-C expression’ section. Brefeldin A (5 μg ml−1) and monensin (1 μg ml−1) were added one hour after the

beginning of the coculture assay, followed by an additional 5 hours of incubation. Cells were stained with viability dye and antibodies against CD3, CD56, KIR2DL1, KIR3DL1, NKG2C and NKG2A. Single-cell proteogenomic profiling of NK cells NK cells were isolated by negative immunomagnetic enrichment (Miltenyi Biotec), blocked with Human TruStain FcX (#422301; BioLegend) for 15 min on ice and then incubated with oligonucleotide-tagged monoclonal antibodies carrying the Totalseq-D modification (Bio- Legend) for 30 min on ice. CD16, CD56, KIR2DL1, KIR3DL1, NKG2C and NKG2A antibodies were used, in addition to a panel of additional oligonucleotide-labeled antibodies described in our previous work76. Two mouse IgG control antibodies (#400299, #400383; BioLegend), conjugated with distinct TotalSeq-D oligonucleotides were included as isotype controls. After three washes with a prechilled cell-staining buffer, cells were filtered with a 40-μm cell Flowmi strainer (#14-100- 150; Thermo Fisher Scientific), counted with an automated cell counter and then loaded into a microfluidic cartridge of the Tapestri analysis platform (Mission Bio) for single-cell multiplex PCR assays. Single-cell amplification of mitochondrial DNA was then performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol94, with minor modifications described in our previous work15,76. Briefly, viable single cells were encapsulated into droplets and lysed. Droplets containing single-cell barcoding beads (tagged with oligonucleotides carrying the cellular barcodes and custom-designed primers) were fused with encapsulated cell lysates. A panel of primers designed to amplify n = 70 adjacent, but nonoverlapping regions of the mitochondrial DNA was then added; primer sequences are summarized in Supplementary Table 7. The droplets were placed under UV light to cleave PCR primers containing unique cell barcodes from beads. To amplify the selected genomic DNA segments and the antibody oligonucleotide tags, droplets were subjected to PCR for 24 cycles with temperature gradients recommended by the manufacturer. Amplification products were then pooled, mixed with AMPure XP beads (#A63882; Beckman Coulter) at a ratio of 0.7, and placed in a magnetic field for separating the DNA and the protein tag libraries. The DNA library bound to AMPure beads was washed with 80% ethanol, while the supernatant containing the protein tag library was aspirated and incubated with a biotinylated oligonucleotide complementary to the 5′ end of the antibody tags, followed by magnetic isolation using streptavidin beads. For library amplification, PCRs were performed with Illumina index primers P5 and P7 on purified DNA and protein libraries, respectively, according to the manufacturer’s protocol; 12 cycles were performed for the DNA library and 18 cycles were run for the protein tag library. The DNA and protein tag libraries were run on a High Sensitivity D1000 ScreenTape instrument (5067- 5584; Agilent Technologies) with the Agilent 4200 TapeStation System to evaluate DNA quality. Libraries were quantified by a fluorometer (Qubit 4.0; Invitrogen) and sequenced on Illumina next-generation

Bioinformatics analysis The Tapestri pipeline (v3.4.0 for NK cells and v2.0.1 for CD4+ T cells; MissionBio) with minor modifications was used to process sequencing data generated by single-cell proteogenomic profiling assays, as described in our prior work15,76. Briefly, for DNA library data, cutadapt (v2.5)95 was used to trim 5′ and 3′ adapter sequences and extract 18 bp cell barcode sequences from Read 1. Cell barcodes that aligned to a unique barcode on a whitelist within a Hamming distance of 2 were used for downstream analysis. Using bwa-mem2 (v2.2.1)96, sequences were aligned to custom reference genomes built from the human genome (hg38), the mitochondrial genome (NC_012920.1) or participant-specific autologous HIV-1 sequences identified in near-full-length proviral sequencing assays, as appropriate. Single-cell alignments were filtered according to criteria implemented in the Tapestri pipeline, and indexed using samtools (v1.19)97. Candidate cells were identified by the CellFinder algorithm built in the Tapestri pipeline. Samtools (v1.19)98 was used to call variants and generate consensus sequences. To reduce spurious alignments, viral sequencing reads were only considered valid if they covered at least 80% of the length of the reference sequence for each given amplicon. MGATK58 was used to call sequence variants in mitochondrial DNA and to calculate the corresponding variant allele frequencies to estimate the level of heteroplasmy; subsequently, scMitoMut99 was utilized to filter and identify mitochondrial mutations that are phylogenetically informative for calling clonal cell lineages. Assessment of NK cell clonality was restricted to cells with no more than one or two high-confidence somatic mutations (VAF ≥ 50%), retaining variants observed in at least five cells. Within these cells, NK cells were considered clonal when they shared the dominant (VAF > 50%) nucleotide variant at polymorphic positions. For identifying cells harboring genome-intact, defective or no HIV-1 DNA, the same criteria were used as described in our prior work15; resulting proviral sequence callings were manually reviewed and edited based on available autologous proviral phylogenetic information. For the analysis of protein library data, cell barcodes were extracted using cutadapt (v2.5). For reads with valid cell barcodes, 15-bp antibody barcodes were extracted from Read 2. Antibody barcode

sequences within a Hamming distance of 1 from known antibody barcodes were accepted. Candidate cells appearing in both libraries were processed for downstream multiomic analysis integrating genotypic and phenotypic data. Read counts for each antibody were normalized to the total read count within each cell using a centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation100. Cutoffs for a given phenotypic marker to be considered positive were defined by marker-specific read counts >1 mean absolute deviation of the normalized median read count corresponding to unspecific IgG control antibodies. To generate a more homogenous cell population for analysis of HIV-1 reservoir cells, CLR values of all candidate cells that were CD3−CD4− (not CD4+ T cells) or CCR7+CD45RA+ (contaminating naive CD4+ T cells) were excluded from proteogenomic CD4 T cell data. Phenotypic analysis was performed using the monocle3 R package101. Antibody read counts were log-transformed, and cells displaying abnormally high IgG read counts or elevated CD3 values were excluded to improve data quality and achieve a more homogeneous cell population. Cells were embedded in two dimensions using UMAP102. To quantify and visualize marker expression of NK cells, median expression values per NK cell clone were calculated and scaled by the mean and standard deviation of cluster means.

Statistics Data are presented as pie charts, bar charts, scatter plots with individual values, UMAP plots, violin plots, Venn diagrams and heatmaps. Differences were tested for statistical significance using two-sided Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank tests, two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests, two-sided Kruskal–Wallis nonparametric tests, two-sided χ tests or Spearman correlation tests, as appropriate. P values of <0.05 were considered statistically significant; FDR correction was performed as described103. Potential synergistic effects between the HLA-C2 allele and specific HLA-E-restricted epitope variants on HIV DNA levels were evaluated using linear regression models incorporating explicit multiplicative interaction terms. Analyses were performed using Prism v10.6 (GraphPad Software, Inc.) and R v4.5104. For evaluating the influence of immunogenetic markers on HIV-1 viral loads and reservoir size (Tables 1 and 2), linear regressions with the function lm() were used in R. Figures were generated using Adobe Illustrator v2026(30.1).
